Line graph titled "Agentic Coding Performance by Effort Level" plotting accuracy percentage against average output tokens per task for five AI models on Z.ai Code Bench v1.0:
 * Claude Fable 5: Highest performance overall, scaling from ~28.8% accuracy at 33K tokens (Low effort) to ~39.4% accuracy at 114K tokens (Max effort).
 * GLM-5.3: Second highest performance, rising sharply from ~24.6% (Low effort) to ~31.3% (High effort) near 49K tokens, peaking at ~34.5% accuracy at 74K tokens (Max effort).
 * GLM-5.3-Flash: Scales from ~21.5% accuracy at 41K tokens (Low effort) to ~29.0% accuracy at 139K tokens (Max effort).
 * Claude Opus 4.8: Scales from ~21.2% accuracy at 28K tokens (Low effort) to ~29.5% accuracy at 120K tokens (Max effort).
 * GLM-5.2: Lowest overall performance, moving from ~19.4% accuracy (Non-Thinking effort at 42K tokens) to ~23.4% accuracy at 94K tokens (Max effort).

Matlin and Chakraborty designed a study » around inf'yence functions, a technique that estimates how much any single training document - an article, post, or page a model trained on - shaped how the model answered a particular benchmark question.
Add those estimates up across the data, and you can see which kinds of writing - literary, technical, and so on - support a given ability in the model. But that holds only if you can confirm the model actually trained on the documents in question.
